findings.summary: Aleph Samach was a Jewish-themed junior honor society at Cornell University, founded in 1893 and active until 1981. It recognized distinct character and emerging leaders among men in their sophomore or junior year, emphasizing leadership, loyalty, service, and honor. The society operated as a stepping stone to senior societies like Sphinx Head and Quill and Dagger, participated in campus governance, and was involved in the 1913-1914 'club war' against social drinking societies. Membership was selective, based on extracurricular participation, and the organization maintained secret rituals. It was last documented active through 1985-86 before becoming defunct.

mechanisms.title: Selection and Tapping
mechanisms.explanation: Students were tapped for membership in Aleph Samach during the spring of their sophomore year or fall of their junior year. Selection criteria focused on participation in extracurricular activities, indicating the society's emphasis on well-rounded campus engagement rather than purely academic metrics.

mechanisms.title: Transition to Senior Societies
mechanisms.explanation: Aleph Samach functioned as a stepping stone to senior honorary societies, specifically Sphinx Head and Quill and Dagger. The society promoted the development of junior leaders who would subsequently be tapped into these senior organizations, which governed broader campus-wide agendas.

unknowns: The specific secret rituals and internal traditions of Aleph Samach, as most ritual details were not documented in publicly available sources.
The precise criteria and process for membership selection beyond the stated focus on extracurricular participation.
The internal dynamics of how Aleph Samach influenced or interacted with the 1913-1914 'club war' beyond the documented alliance with other societies.
The exact reasons and timeline for the society's transition from active status to defunct status after 1985, despite documented activity in the late 1980s.
